items.new: Meanwhile he kept on undressing, and at last uncovered his chest and arms. As I live, those hidden parts of him were checkered with the same squares as his face; his back was covered in the same dark squares too; he looked as if he had fought in a Thirty Years' War and just escaped with a shirt of sticking plaster. What's more, even his legs were marked, as if a crowd of dark green frogs were running up the trunks of young palm trees. It was now perfectly clear that he must be some abominable savage or other who had signed onto a whaler in the South Seas and so ended up in this Christian country. I shook at the thought. A head-peddler, too — maybe the heads of his own brothers. He might take a liking to mine — heavens! Look at that tomahawk!

items.new: After supper and another sociable chat and smoke, we went to our room together. He gave me his embalmed head as a present; then he took out his huge tobacco pouch, felt around under the tobacco, and pulled out about thirty dollars in silver. Spreading the coins on the table, he mechanically split them into two equal piles, pushed one toward me, and said it was mine. I was about to object, but he cut me off by pouring them into my trouser pockets. I let them stay there. Then he began his evening prayers, took out his idol, and removed the papered fire-board. From certain signs and hints, I thought he seemed eager for me to join him; but knowing perfectly well what would follow, I considered for a moment whether, if he asked me, I would go along with it or not.

items.new: On this one point Ahab seemed no different from most American whaling captains, who, as a class, tend to think the ship's cabin belongs to them by right, and that anyone else is allowed in it only as a courtesy. So, in plain truth, the mates and harpooners of the Pequod could more accurately be said to have lived outside the cabin than in it. For when they did go in, it was rather the way a street door goes into a house: it swings inward for a moment, only to be swung back out the next, and it lives, permanently, in the open air. Not that they lost much by this; there was no companionship in the cabin; socially, Ahab was unapproachable. Though he was nominally counted in the census of Christendom, he was still a stranger to it. He lived in the world the way the last of the grizzly bears lived in settled Missouri. And just as, when spring and summer had gone, that wild Logan of the woods would bury himself in a hollow tree and live out the winter there, sucking his own paws, so in his harsh, howling old age Ahab's soul, shut up in the hollowed trunk of his body, fed there on the sullen paws of its gloom!
